all_historical_figures.name: Rāmānuja
all_historical_figures.significance: His influence helped popularize the Pāñcarātra system in South India.

all_historical_figures.name: Pāṇini
all_historical_figures.significance: His work refers to the Vṛṣṇi tribe, providing an early literary reference to the group from which Vāsudeva emerged.

all_historical_figures.name: Patañjali
all_historical_figures.significance: He mentions Vāsudeva (Kṛṣṇa) by name, confirming his revered status.

all_historical_figures.name: Vāsudeva (Kṛṣṇa)
all_historical_figures.role: Central deity of the Bhāgavata cult
all_historical_figures.significance: Identified with the supreme Godhead Nārāyaṇa; originally a human hero of the Vṛṣṇi clan who was deified.

all_historical_figures.name: Nārāyaṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: A Vedic deity (seer of the Puruṣa-sūkta) who becomes identified with Vāsudeva.

all_historical_figures.name: Saṃkarṣaṇa (Baladeva)
all_historical_figures.significance: One of the earliest deified heroes alongside Vāsudeva; later becomes the second vyūha.

all_historical_figures.name: Viśvaksena
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as one of the heroes of the tribe.

all_historical_figures.name: Sarva-tāta
all_historical_figures.significance: Built a stone temple for Vāsudeva and Saṃkarṣaṇa, as recorded in the Nāgarī inscription, and called himself a 'bhāgavata'.

all_historical_figures.name: Heliodorus
all_historical_figures.significance: Erected the Besnagar column for Vāsudeva and declared himself a 'bhāgavata', showing the cult's appeal to non-Indians.

all_historical_figures.name: Dion
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in the Besnagar inscription.

all_historical_figures.name: Antialikdas
all_historical_figures.significance: Sent Heliodorus as an ambassador.

all_historical_figures.name: Kāśīputra-bhāgabhadra
all_historical_figures.significance: Received the ambassador Heliodorus at his court.

all_historical_figures.name: Gupta Monarchs (Samudragupta, Chandragupta II, Kumāragupta I)
all_historical_figures.significance: Styled themselves 'bhāgavatas' and 'parama-bhāgavatas', indicating the cult's royal patronage.

all_historical_figures.name: Toṣā
all_historical_figures.significance: Commissioned a temple and icons for the five Vṛṣṇi heroes, as recorded in the Morā well inscription.

all_historical_figures.name: Śoḍāśa-svāmi
all_historical_figures.significance: Reigned during the time of the Morā well and another Mathurā inscription dedicated to Vāsudeva.

all_historical_figures.name: Pradyumna, Sāmba, Aniruddha
all_historical_figures.significance: Part of the 'five heroes' (pañcavīras) worshipped in the Vīra-vāda cult; later incorporated into the vyūha system.

all_historical_figures.name: Nara and Nārāyaṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: Original teachers of the Bhāgavata doctrine in their hermitage at Badari; represent the manifest Prakṛti and Puruṣa.

all_historical_figures.name: Nārada
all_historical_figures.significance: Learned the Pāñcarātra doctrine from Nārāyaṇa and transmitted it to the world.

all_historical_figures.name: Uparicara
all_historical_figures.significance: A great devotee of Nārāyaṇa who lived according to 'Sāttvata-vidhi' and patronized Pāñcarātra scholars.

all_historical_figures.name: The Seven Sages (Marīci, Atri, Aṅgirasa, etc.)
all_historical_figures.significance: Credited with crystallizing the Pāñcarātra system for the benefit of humanity.

all_historical_figures.name: Kapila
all_historical_figures.significance: Considered an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa, linking Sāṃkhya to the Bhāgavata tradition.

all_historical_figures.name: Āsuri
all_historical_figures.significance: Successor to Kapila.

all_historical_figures.name: Pañca-śikha
all_historical_figures.significance: Disciple of Āsuri; described in the epic as being proficient in both Sāṃkhya and Pāñcarātra.

all_historical_figures.name: Vivasvān
all_historical_figures.significance: First recipient of the 'yoga' teaching (Bhāgavata doctrine) from Kṛṣṇa/Nārāyaṇa.

all_historical_figures.name: Manu
all_historical_figures.significance: Received the teaching from Vivasvān and passed it on.

all_historical_figures.name: Ikṣvāku
all_historical_figures.role: Son of Manu, founder of the solar dynasty
all_historical_figures.significance: Received the teaching from Manu and spread it in the world.

all_historical_figures.name: Pañcaśikha
all_historical_figures.significance: Visited the court of Janaka in Mithilā, showing the doctrine's presence in epic times.

all_historical_figures.name: Janaka
all_historical_figures.significance: Hosted the sage Pañcaśikha.

all_historical_figures.name: Nārāyaṇa / Vāsudeva / Viṣṇu / Kṛṣṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: The central object of worship and the divine source of the Pāñcarātra teachings.

all_historical_figures.name: Vedānta-deśika
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of Pāñcarātra-rakṣā; his classification of texts and views on the Sāttvata-saṁhitā are cited.

all_historical_figures.name: The Five Sages (as weapon incarnations)
all_historical_figures.significance: Mythological figures (Śāṇḍilya, Kauśika, Bhāradvāja, Mauñjyāyana, Aupagāyana) who represent the human transmission of divine knowledge.

all_historical_figures.name: Brahmā, Śiva, Ananta, Viśvaksena, Garuḍa, Indra
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as promulgators or recipients of the Pāñcarātra teachings in various origin stories.

all_historical_figures.name: Nārada
all_historical_figures.significance: Consistently identified as the first and foremost human recipient and teacher of the Pāñcarātra doctrine.

all_historical_figures.name: The Seven Sages (Sanaka, etc.)
all_historical_figures.significance: Taught by Nārada; considered the first masters and exponents of the teaching.

all_historical_figures.name: Marīci, Atri, Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Svāyambhuva
all_historical_figures.significance: Received the teaching directly from Nārāyaṇa; their Samhitās are classified as Sāttvika.

all_historical_figures.name: Āḻvārs
all_historical_figures.significance: Their hymns (Divya Prabandham) eulogize the 'divya-deśas' (sacred temples) where Pāñcarātra worship is conducted.

all_historical_figures.name: Śrī-Śaila-Veṅkaṭa-Sudhi
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of the 14th-century text Siddhānta-ratnākara.

all_historical_figures.name: Otto Schräder
all_historical_figures.significance: Enumerated 215 Pāñcarātra-Samhitās in his 1916 introduction to Ahirbudhnya-Samhitā.

all_historical_figures.name: V. Kriṣṇamācārya
all_historical_figures.significance: Edited Lakṣmī-tantra (1975) and listed 225 saṁhitās.

all_historical_figures.name: Alasiṅga-bhaṭṭa
all_historical_figures.significance: Wrote an important commentary (bhāṣya) on the Sāttvata-saṁhitā and a gloss on the Īśvara-saṁhitā.

all_historical_figures.name: Yogananda-narasimha-bhaṭṭa
all_historical_figures.significance: Father of Alasiṅga-bhaṭṭa; authored Sāttvatāmṛta.

all_historical_figures.name: Rāmānuja
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited the ancient Pauṣkara-samhitā, establishing its antiquity.

all_historical_figures.name: Nṛsiṁha-yajvā
all_historical_figures.significance: Wrote a commentary on the Pārameśvara-saṁhitā.

all_historical_figures.name: Peddaṇṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: Prepared a gloss (Pāñcarātra-pradīpikā) on the Pādma-saṁhitā.

all_historical_figures.name: Saṁkarṣaṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: Identified as the first official master of the Sāttvata creed who taught Śāṇḍilya.

all_historical_figures.name: Paraśu-rāma
all_historical_figures.significance: Asked Nārada to teach the path of ritualistic action in the Sāttvata-saṁhitā.

all_historical_figures.name: Yāmuna-muni
all_historical_figures.role: Great Śrī-vaiṣṇava teacher, predecessor of Rāmānuja
all_historical_figures.significance: Authored 'Āgama-prāmāṇya' to defend the authoritative character of Pāñcarātra and attempt a reconciliation with the Vedic tradition.

all_historical_figures.name: Rāmānuja
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned to provide context for Yāmuna-muni's timeline and lineage.

all_historical_figures.name: Vedān-ta-deśika (Veṅkaṭanātha)
all_historical_figures.significance: Authored 'Pāñcarātra-rakṣa', providing an elaborate defense of the Pāñcarātra system centuries after Yāmuna-muni, showing the persistence of the conflict. He argued Pāñcarātra was rooted in the Veda.

all_historical_figures.name: Śāṇḍilya
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited as an example of a sage who came to prefer the Pāñcarātra (Sāttvata) mode of worship over Vedic methods.

all_historical_figures.name: Jamadagni
all_historical_figures.significance: His 'smṛti' is quoted as prescribing worship with Vedic mantras preferably, but allowing Pāñcarātra hymns when Vedic mantras are unavailable.

all_historical_figures.name: Kapila
all_historical_figures.significance: Credited with crystallizing the Sāṁkhya system, one of the five fundamental disciplines mentioned in the Ahirbudhnya-saṁhitā. Also mentioned as a four-faced composite deity in the Tantrāntara-siddhānta.

all_historical_figures.name: Hiraṇya-garbha
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as the originator of the Yoga system, one of the five fundamental disciplines.

all_historical_figures.name: Ahirbudhnya
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as the originator of the Pāśupata school, one of the five fundamental disciplines.

all_historical_figures.name: Sudar-śana
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as the originator of the Pāñcarātra (Sāt-tvata) system, one of the five fundamental disciplines.

all_historical_figures.name: Patañjali
all_historical_figures.significance: His work is referenced for containing the term 'Śiva-bhāgavatas', suggesting an attempt to include devotees of Śiva within the broader Pāñcarātra fold.

all_historical_figures.name: Aupagāyana
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as one of the sages initiated by Brahmā into the mantra-siddhānta.

all_historical_figures.name: Yāmuna-muni
all_historical_figures.significance: Attempted to integrate Viśiṣṭādvaita ideas with Pāñcarātra. Authored 'Āgama-prāmāṇya' to establish the authority of Pāñcarātra texts. Quoted several Pāñcarātra saṁhitās.

all_historical_figures.name: Rāmānuja
all_historical_figures.significance: Attempted to integrate Viśiṣṭādvaita ideas with Pāñcarātra. Quoted from Pāñcarātra works like Sāttvata-, Pauṣkara-, Parama-saṁhitās and Lakṣmī-tantra.

all_historical_figures.name: Vedānta-deśika
all_historical_figures.significance: Attempted to integrate Viśiṣṭādvaita ideas with Pāñcarātra. Authored 'Saccaritra-rakṣā' and 'Pāñcarātra-rakṣā'. Referred to Pāñcarātra as 'ekāyana-śruti'.

all_historical_figures.name: Piļļai-Lokācārya
all_historical_figures.significance: Attempted to integrate Viśiṣṭādvaita ideas with Pāñcarātra. Authored 'Tattva-traya'.

all_historical_figures.name: Vara-vara-muni
all_historical_figures.significance: Attempted to integrate Viśiṣṭādvaita ideas with Pāñcarātra.

all_historical_figures.name: Śāṇḍilya
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited as an example of one who was dissatisfied with the Vedic tradition and found fulfilment in the Sāttvata-vidhi.

all_historical_figures.name: Śaṁkara
all_historical_figures.significance: Referred to and discussed the tenets of the 'pāñcarātra-siddhānta' in his commentary on the Vedānta-sūtra (2,2,44), indicating Pāñcarātra was a well-defined system in his time.

all_historical_figures.name: Utpala-Vaiṣṇava
all_historical_figures.significance: Contemporary of Abhinava-gupta. Knew of Pāñcarātra-śruti, Pāñcarātropaniṣat, and Pāñcarātra-śāstra. Cited numerous Pāñcarātra works.

all_historical_figures.name: Utpala-deva
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned to distinguish him from Utpala-Vaiṣṇava. Author of 'Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya' and disciple of Somānandra.

all_historical_figures.name: Somānandra
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of 'Śiva-dṛṣṭi' and teacher of Utpala-deva.

all_historical_figures.name: Abhinava-gupta
all_historical_figures.significance: His dates are used to place his contemporary, Utpala-Vaiṣṇava.

all_historical_figures.name: Kṣemarāja
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of 'Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya'. Mentioned the Pāñcarātra ideology regarding transcendental prakṛti as Vāsudeva.

all_historical_figures.name: Otto Schrader
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of 'Introduction to the Pāñcarātra'. His interpretations of several Pāñcarātra technical terms ('vidyā', 'Kāla-saṁhitā', 'Kartavya', 'Vaiśeṣika') are explicitly refuted by the author of this chapter.

all_historical_figures.name: Patañjali
all_historical_figures.significance: His definition of yoga (from root 'yuj' - concentration) is contrasted with the Pāñcarātra definition (from root 'yujir' - union). His eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga) yoga is identified with the Sāttvata-yoga in Ahirbudhnya-saṁhitā.

all_historical_figures.name: Alasinga-bhaṭṭa
all_historical_figures.significance: His interpretation of 'kriyā-mārga' in the Sāttvata-saṁhitā is mentioned, though the author notes it is not supported by the original text.

all_historical_figures.name: Parāśara-bhaṭṭa
all_historical_figures.significance: A key commentator on Viṣṇu-sahasra-nāma-stotra whose interpretations on the three modes of the Deity are cited as authoritative.

all_historical_figures.name: Ālasiṅga-bhaṭṭa
all_historical_figures.significance: Commentator on the Sāttvata-saṃhitā, whose explanations are referenced, particularly regarding the list of vibhava forms.

all_historical_figures.name: Otto Schräder
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned for having erroneously identified 39 vibhava forms in the Sāttvata-saṃhitā, a point the author corrects.

all_historical_figures.name: Brahmā
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as the four-faced creator produced during the 'mixed creation' phase of Aniruddha. Also personified in the vibhava form Vidyādhideva.

all_historical_figures.name: Vyāsa
all_historical_figures.significance: Classified as an 'āveśāvatāra' (divine possession). Also appears as the vibhava form 'Veda-vit', who classified the Vedas.

all_historical_figures.name: Arjuna
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as an 'āveśāvatāra' and the recipient of the revelation of the Viśva-rūpa form in Kurkṣetra.

all_historical_figures.name: Kṛṣṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: Appears in multiple contexts: as an avatāra from Aniruddha, as 'Pārijāta-hara', and as one of the four ascetic sons of Dharma. His classification as 'sākṣāt' or 'āveśa' is noted as a point of discussion.

all_historical_figures.name: Rāma
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as Śrī-rāma, an avatāra who destroyed Rāvaṇa. His classification is also debated.

all_historical_figures.name: Buddha
all_historical_figures.significance: Appears as the vibhava form 'Loka-nātha'. His status as a direct or possessed incarnation (sākṣāt vs āveśāvatāra) is shown as a point of difference between texts.

all_historical_figures.name: Śiva
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as being empowered to destroy and as part of the composite Dattātreya incarnation.

all_historical_figures.name: Dattātreya
all_historical_figures.significance: Listed as a vibhava form, a composite incarnation of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.

all_historical_figures.name: Ānanda- tīrtha (Madhvācārya)
all_historical_figures.role: Author of Tantra-sāra-saṅgraha, great ācārya, founder of the Vedāntic system of Tattva-vāda
all_historical_figures.significance: His philosophy forms the entire ideological basis of the Tantra-sārāgama discussed in the chapter.

all_historical_figures.name: Śaṃkara
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as one of the three great ācāryas of Vedānta, providing historical context for Madhvācārya.

all_historical_figures.name: Rāmānuja
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as one of the three great ācāryas of Vedānta, providing historical context for Madhvācārya.

all_historical_figures.name: Viṣṇu-tīrtha
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of 'Ṣoḍaśī' and 'Caturdaśī', texts cited to explain the concepts of bimba and mental worship.

complete_timeline.significance: His activities led to the increased popularity of Pāñcarātra in South India.

complete_timeline.event: Expounding of the Vedāntic system and founding of the sect by Ānanda-tīrtha (Madhvācārya)
complete_timeline.significance: Established the Tattva-vāda philosophy which is the foundation of the Tantra-sārāgama.
A key commentary on the Īśvara-saṁhitā, indicating active scholarly work on these texts in the 19th century.
Published by the Asiatic Society of Bengal, it was one of the earliest Pāñcarātra texts to be printed, though it is now considered atypical of the tradition.

complete_timeline.event: Publication of Otto Schräder's Introduction to Ahirbudhnya-Samhitā
complete_timeline.significance: Provided a critical scholarly list of 215 Pāñcarātra texts, forming a basis for modern studies.

complete_timeline.event: Publication of V. Kriṣṇamācārya's edition of Lakṣmī-tantra
complete_timeline.significance: Contributed an updated list of 225 Pāñcarātra saṁhitās, expanding on earlier scholarly work.
A modern printed edition from Varanasi, making this foundational text more accessible.
Records the reconstruction of a 'Bhāgavata' shrine.
During this period, Pāñcarātra was already a 'well-defined system of thought', as evidenced by Śaṁkara's discussion of it in his Vedānta-sūtra commentary.
This period shows that Pāñcarātra texts and concepts were known and cited by Kāśmīri writers, indicating the system's influence and established status.
Kṣemarāja's work 'Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya' mentions specific Pāñcarātra doctrines, showing its continued relevance and interaction with other philosophical schools like Kashmir Shaivism.
Demonstrates that the debate over Pāñcarātra's authenticity continued for centuries and required new, elaborate defenses by later Śrī-vaiṣṇava leaders.
A landmark effort to establish the scriptural authority of the Pāñcarātra Āgamas and reconcile them with the Vedic tradition.
His commentary explicitly mentions the worship of Vāsudeva.
His work provides the earliest literary reference to the Vṛṣṇi tribe.
The Morā well inscription, recording a temple for the five Vṛṣṇi heroes, was created during his reign.
The Bhāgavata cult received royal patronage, with emperors calling themselves 'bhāgavatas' on their coins.

complete_timeline.event: Creation of the Burhikhar village inscription
complete_timeline.significance: Records the gift of a four-armed image of Bhagavān (Vāsudeva).

complete_timeline.event: Creation of the Nāgarī and Besnagar inscriptions
complete_timeline.significance: Provide the earliest epigraphic evidence for temples and worship dedicated to Vāsudeva (and Saṃkarṣaṇa), and the use of the term 'bhāgavata' by devotees, including a Greek ambassador.

all_geographic_locations.context: Region where Pāñcarātra is most popular, especially after Rāmānuja.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A key geographical center for the Pāñcarātra tradition.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of an inscription from the 2nd-1st century B.C. about a temple to Vāsudeva and Saṃkarṣaṇa.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Site of early epigraphic evidence for the Bhāgavata cult.

all_geographic_locations.place: Besnagar (Vidiśā, near Gwālior in Madhya Pradesh)
all_geographic_locations.context: Location of the Heliodorus pillar inscription from the 2nd century B.C.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Crucial evidence for the early spread and prestige of the Bhāgavata cult, attracting foreign devotees.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of a 402 A.D. inscription recording the reconstruction of a 'Bhāgavata' shrine.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Shows continued patronage and activity of the cult into the Gupta period.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of an inscription recording the construction of a temple for the five Vṛṣṇi heroes.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Evidence for the 'Vīra-vāda' or cult of the five heroes.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of a 1st century B.C. inscription recording the gift of a four-armed image of Bhagavān.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Early evidence for the iconography of Viṣṇu/Vāsudeva.

all_geographic_locations.context: The holy hermitage in the Himālayan heights where sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa resided.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Mythical origin point of the Pāñcarātra teaching.

all_geographic_locations.context: A mythical island on the northern side of the Milky Ocean (Kṣīrābdhi) where Nārada received the Pāñcarātra doctrine from Nārāyaṇa.
all_geographic_locations.significance: The celestial locus of the perfect, 'ekāntin' devotees and the source of the divine revelation.

all_geographic_locations.context: The location of King Janaka's court, where the Sāṃkhyan teacher Pañca-śikha visited.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A setting in the epic that demonstrates the interaction between Sāṃkhya and royal courts.

all_geographic_locations.context: Court of King Janaka, visited by the Pāñcarātra expert Pañcaśikha.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Indicates the geographical reach and influence of the doctrine during the epic period.

all_geographic_locations.context: Sacred spot where Sudarśana (discus) appeared as the sage Śāṇḍilya.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A mythological location for the origin of one of the five teaching streams.

all_geographic_locations.context: Sacred spot where Pāñcajanya (conch) appeared as the sage Kauśika.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A mythological location for the origin of one of the five teaching streams.

all_geographic_locations.context: Sacred spot where Kaumodakī (mace) appeared as the sage Bhāradvāja.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A mythological location for the origin of one of the five teaching streams.

all_geographic_locations.context: Sacred spot where Nandaka (sword) appeared as the sage Mauñjyāyana.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A mythological location for the origin of one of the five teaching streams.

all_geographic_locations.context: Sacred spot where Śārṅga (bow) appeared as the sage Aupagāyana.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A mythological location for the origin of one of the five teaching streams.

all_geographic_locations.context: The celestial abode where Nārada received the teaching from Nārāyaṇa.
all_geographic_locations.significance: The divine source location of the Pāñcarātra doctrine.

all_geographic_locations.context: Temple of Nārāyaṇa where the Sāttvata-saṁhitā is traditionally followed.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A major center for the Sāttvata tradition in South India.

all_geographic_locations.context: Famous Ranganātha temple where the Pauṣkara-saṁhitā is traditionally followed.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A preeminent Śrīvaiṣṇava center associated with the Pauṣkara tradition.

all_geographic_locations.context: The Varadarāja temple where the Jayākhya-saṁhitā is traditionally followed.
all_geographic_locations.significance: An important Vaiṣṇava center associated with the Jayākhya tradition.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location where Nārada communicated the teaching of Vāsudeva to the sages.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Site of the human-to-human transmission of the doctrine.

all_geographic_locations.context: Celestial realm where Śiva and Nārada had the dialogue recorded in the Nārada-pāñcarātra.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Mythological setting for the atypical Nārada-pāñcarātra text.

all_geographic_locations.context: Place where Nārada recalled his dialogue with Śiva.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Earthly setting for the narration of the Nārada-pāñcarātra.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned in relation to Buddhist tantrik cults that worship lion-faced, hog-headed, and multi-faced deities.
all_geographic_locations.significance: The author suggests a probable influence of these distant tantrik cults on the 'tantrāntara' siddhānta of Pāñcarātra, which features similar composite deities.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned in relation to writers Utpala-Vaiṣṇava, Utpala-deva, and Kṣemarāja.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Indicates a region where Pāñcarātra philosophy was known, studied, and interacted with other major philosophical schools like Kashmir Shaivism.

all_geographic_locations.context: Publication location of Otto Schrader's 'Introduction to the Pāñcarātra'.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Context for modern Indological scholarship on Pāñcarātra.

all_geographic_locations.context: The transcendental realm (paramam dhāma), the high heavens where the 'para' mode of the Deity resides.
all_geographic_locations.significance: It is the ultimate goal for emancipated souls (muktas) and the abode of eternal masters (nitya-sūris).

all_geographic_locations.context: The battlefield where the Viśva-rūpa (cosmic form) was revealed to Arjuna.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A key site for a major divine revelation mentioned in the Mahābhārata and Bhagavad-gītā.

all_geographic_locations.context: A mythical island where the Viśva-rūpa was revealed to Nārada and where the Vihangama (Haṃsa) form abides.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A sacred place associated with divine manifestations in Pāñcarātra and Puranic literature.

all_geographic_locations.context: The place where the Dharma-mūrti form of the Deity becomes manifest.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A sacred forest associated with the personification of Dharma.

all_geographic_locations.context: The lowest of the netherworlds where Kamatheśvara (Kūrma) abides.
all_geographic_locations.significance: The cosmic foundation, supported by an incarnation of Viṣṇu.

all_geographic_locations.context: The celestial garden from which the Pārijāta-flower was snatched by Kṛṣṇa (in his Pārijāta-hara form).
all_geographic_locations.significance: The setting for a famous mythological episode involving Kṛṣṇa.

all_geographic_locations.context: The region of Magadha, mentioned in a quote as where the Loka-nātha (Buddha) form is situated.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Historically associated with the life and teachings of the Buddha.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as the location of a crooked mango tree, which is cited as an example of a secondary divine manifestation (gauṇa).
all_geographic_locations.significance: A location in the Rāmāyaṇa, used here to illustrate the all-pervasiveness of divine intention.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of temples where Tantra-sārāgama is practiced.
all_geographic_locations.significance: General region of the tradition's prevalence.

all_geographic_locations.context: Coastal regions where the worship according to Tantra-sārāgama is especially conducted.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Specific geographical heartland of this Āgama tradition.

complete_terminology_index.context: The Pāñcarātra is described as one of the Āgama divisions devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.
The most popular Āgama division for Viṣṇu worship, identified with the Bhāgavata cult.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Related to Bhagavān (the Lord); a devotee of Bhagavān
complete_terminology_index.context: The name of the cult centered on Nārāyaṇa/Vāsudeva. Also used to describe a devotee, like King Sarva-tāta and Heliodorus.

complete_terminology_index.translation: The tradition centered on the worship of Viṣṇu
complete_terminology_index.context: The broader religious framework into which the Bhāgavata cult developed.

complete_terminology_index.translation: A member of the warrior or ruling class
complete_terminology_index.context: Vāsudeva is described as a human hero and a kṣattriya who was deified.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Name of a tribe or clan
complete_terminology_index.context: The clan to which Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa belonged.

complete_terminology_index.translation: An alternative name for the Vṛṣṇi clan
complete_terminology_index.context: The doctrine is called Sāttvata-vidhi, and the tradition is Sāttvata-tantra.
The title for the supreme Godhead, Nārāyaṇa.
Title given to Vāsudeva in the Besnagar inscription.

complete_terminology_index.translation: A column or standard topped with Garuḍa
complete_terminology_index.context: The Besnagar inscription is on such a column, a symbol of Viṣṇu.
The initial cult of the deified five heroes of the Vṛṣṇi clan.
The doctrine of four divine emanations (Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha) that developed in Bhāgavata ideology.

complete_terminology_index.translation: The scripture of the Bhagavātas/of Bhagavān
complete_terminology_index.context: A name for the Pāñcarātra system.

complete_terminology_index.translation: A collection of six divine attributes
complete_terminology_index.context: Bhagavān is the possessor of bhaga (jñāna, śakti, bala, aiśvarya, vīrya, tejas).

complete_terminology_index.translation: The Veda which is the one/only path
complete_terminology_index.context: A name for the Pāñcarātra doctrine, signifying it as the sole path to salvation.
A claim made by Pāñcarātra that its teaching is the primordial Veda from which others branched.
The doctrine taught by Saṃkarṣaṇa and associated with Pāñcarātra.
The ten incarnations of Viṣṇu enumerated in the Nārāyaṇīya.
The term for the ideal devotee in the Bhāgavata-Pāñcarātra tradition.
The central practice and distinguishing feature of the Bhāgavata cult.

complete_terminology_index.translation: One of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy, focusing on knowledge/enumeration
complete_terminology_index.context: The Bhāgavata cult is said to be deeply associated with its doctrines.

A sacrifice performed by Puruṣa-Nārāyaṇa in the Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa, which is seen as a Vedic precursor to the Pāñcarātra system.
The central term, its meaning is the main subject of the first section, evolving from a literal to a doctrinal sense.
Refers to the original five-night sacrifice mentioned in the Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa.

complete_terminology_index.translation: One who has a single object of devotion
complete_terminology_index.context: A term for the bhāgavatas, who were exclusively devoted to the worship of Nārāyaṇa.
The five-fold division of the day for religious duties: abhigamana, upādāna, ijyā, svādhyāya, and yoga.
The first phase of pañca-kāla, early morning preparatory sequences.
The second phase of pañca-kāla, collecting articles for worship.
The third and most important phase of pañca-kāla, the formal iconic worship.
The fourth phase of pañca-kāla, devoted to the study of scriptures.
The fifth phase of pañca-kāla, practice and deep meditation at night.
The second part of 'pāñcarātra', given numerous interpretations in different texts.
The five celestial weapons of Viṣṇu, whose incarnations were the five sages who received the teaching.
The highest class of Pāñcarātra texts, considered to be of divine origin.
The second class of texts, composed by sages.
The third and least authoritative class of texts.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Related to the qualities of purity, passion, and darkness
complete_terminology_index.context: The three guṇas used to sub-classify the muni-prokta texts.
A metrical unit of thirty-two syllables, used to measure the extent of the literature.
A type of text in the Pāñcarātra corpus, a compilation or treatise.
The primordial scripture of pure devotion from which Pāñcarātra is said to originate.
The central practical path of Pāñcarātra, focusing on temple building, icon making, and worship.
A section or division of an Āgama text, ideally four in number (Jñāna, Yoga, Kriyā, Caryā).
The main subject of the chapter.
The tradition of teachers like Yāmuna-muni and Rāmānuja who defended Pāñcarātra.
Title of Yāmuna-muni's treatise defending Pāñcarātra.

Title of Vedānta-deśika's treatise.

A Pāñcarātra critique of the Vedas.

Another name for the Pāñcarātra system.
The easier and more effective path emphasized by Pāñcarātra.

Term used in Kūrma and Skanda Purāṇas to describe Pāñcarātra and other schools.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Releasing the individual soul (paśu) from bondage (pāśa).
complete_terminology_index.context: The goal of the Pāśupata school.
A term from Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya suggesting attempts to integrate Śaiva devotees.
The term for the major divisions within the Pāñcarātra system.
The frowned-upon practice of mixing the rituals and doctrines of different siddhāntas.

complete_terminology_index.translation: The first of the four cosmic ages.
complete_terminology_index.context: The age when āgama-siddhānta is said to have appeared.
The principal mode of worship in mantra-siddhānta.
The four divine emanations (Vāsudeva, Saṁkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha) central to āgama-siddhānta.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Fullness of the six divine attributes.
complete_terminology_index.context: The attributes (bala, vīrya, etc.) that define the vyūha forms.

Injunctions (abhigamana, upādāna, etc.) followed meticulously in āgama-siddhānta.
The mode of worship characterizing the tantra and tantrāntara siddhāntas.

Emanations involving other guṇas, like Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Literally 'five nights'. Name of the Vaishnava Agama system being discussed.
complete_terminology_index.context: The central subject of the chapter.

complete_terminology_index.translation: The one path Veda, or original Veda.
complete_terminology_index.context: Pāñcarātra's claim to be the original Veda from which the other four ('vikāra-vedas') emerged.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Rule or prescription of the Sāttvatas (devotees of Viṣṇu).
complete_terminology_index.context: Describes the practical, worship-oriented nature of the Pāñcarātra system.
A simpler technique for salvation introduced into later Pāñcarātra under Viśiṣṭādvaita influence.
Synonymous with prapatti, described as a six-fold path (ṣaḍaṅga).
One of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy; provides the theoretical foundation for early Pāñcarātra.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Nature, matter, the material cause of the universe.
complete_terminology_index.context: A core concept from Sāṁkhya used extensively in Pāñcarātra cosmology.

The primary emanations of God in Pāñcarātra theology (Vāsudeva, Saṁkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha).

complete_terminology_index.translation: That which is heard; revealed scripture (the Vedas).
complete_terminology_index.context: Pāñcarātra is described as 'ekāyana-śruti', claiming revealed status.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Possessor of 'bhaga' (majesty, auspicious qualities); the adorable one, God.
complete_terminology_index.context: A key term for Godhead in the Pāñcarātra system.

Systematized and spiritual knowledge, identified with the energy of Godhead.
Mental worship or contemplation, as distinguished from external rituals (bahir-yajña).
The final goal in the Pāñcarātra system, described as a positive state of attainment.

The act of divine grace that initiates the process of liberation for a soul.
The highest form of liberation, defined as union with Godhead.

The highest, ultimate, and formless mode of the Deity.

complete_terminology_index.context: A core concept; refers to Viṣṇu as the original reality of which the soul is a reflection.

complete_terminology_index.translation: A counterpart, a reflection, an image
